notes.meaning: After the deadly plague at Peor had ended, the Lord spoke to Moses and Eleazar the priest. Aaron had died earlier, so his son Eleazar now served as high priest in his place. This command marked a turning point, showing that the doomed older generation had passed away and the new generation was ready to move forward.

God ordered a new count of all Israelite men twenty years old and older who could fight in the army. This census proved that God had kept His promise to multiply Abraham's descendants, even after severe judgments in the desert. It also prepared the leaders to divide the Promised Land fairly among the tribes based on their size.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see these census figures as symbolic or idealized rather than literal counts, arguing that the wilderness could not support over two million people.

notes.meaning: Moses and Eleazar delivered God's command while camped on the plains of Moab, right across the Jordan River from Jericho. The thirty-eight years of wandering were finished, and the people stood on the very edge of the Promised Land. The leaders instructed the tribe heads to register every fighting man, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.

Reuben was Jacob's firstborn son, and his tribe was registered by its four main clans: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. In all, the fighting men of Reuben numbered 43,730. This was a drop of nearly three thousand men from their first count at Sinai, partly because many were lost in earlier rebellions.

The family record pauses at Pallu's son Eliab to mention his sons Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram. Dathan and Abiram were well-known leaders chosen by the people, but they used their standing to challenge Moses and Aaron during Korah's revolt. By fighting against God's appointed leaders, they were actually rebelling against the Lord Himself.

The ground split open and swallowed Dathan, Abiram, and their households, while divine fire burned up the two hundred and fifty men who offered incense with Korah. Their sudden end served as an unmistakable warning sign for the entire nation. It stood as a permanent reminder never to rise up in pride against God's appointed order.

Korah's family line was not wiped out with him. His sons chose not to take part in their father's rebellion, and God spared their lives. Many years later, their descendants served as musicians and gatekeepers in God's temple and wrote several of the Psalms.

Simeon's descendants were listed under five major clans, totaling only 22,200 men. This was a crushing loss of over thirty-seven thousand soldiers since the first census at Sinai. Because a Simeonite prince had led the people into the recent sin at Baal-peor, many in this tribe likely died in that plague.

The tribe of Gad was organized into seven clans: Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ozni, Eri, Arod, and Areli. These groups matched the sons of Gad who originally went down to Egypt. God preserved each family's identity so they could receive their own piece of the land.

The registered fighting men of Gad totaled 40,500. This was a decrease of more than five thousand soldiers compared to their first count at Sinai. Even after this loss, Gad remained a strong and ready part of Israel's military force.

Judah's first two sons, Er and Onan, are named only to explain why no clans came from them. They died in the land of Canaan long before the Israelites went to Egypt because the Lord judged them for their wickedness. Since they died childless, they left no families to be numbered.

Judah's remaining sons formed three main clans through Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. The family of Perez became so large that it split into two additional clans named after his sons, Hezron and Hamul. Even though Judah had faced painful family losses in Canaan, God showed great mercy by multiplying his remaining line.

The clans of Judah numbered 76,500 fighting men, making Judah the largest of all the tribes. While the tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad had all shrunk during the wilderness years, Judah gained nearly two thousand men. This steady growth reflected God's special favor and blessing on the tribe that was chosen to lead Israel.
